changes: Warm-ups sit where the day's work is (the spider at frets 5 to 8, where position 1 lives), not anywhere on the neck.
Each why says what the drill trains and why it works ("a power chord is a root and its 5th, so every chord is a new place for the shape"), not only what it improves.
Done is a feel ("until the new chord lands on beat 1 without a gap"), never a count, and one-minute changes are rounds, not a tally.
Blocks end with a turn of the student's own: a riff from two notes, an ending of their choice, last week's A phrase moved to E.
Day 7 asks the student to make up a position drill by changing one thing, the way every drill this week did.

Triads and double stops (grip steps in a play-along) replace two spider warm-ups and the plain roots-and-5ths drill: day 2 splits power chords into notes and finds the double stops in position 1, day 4 plays G C D as triads on two string sets, day 6 mixes triads, single notes and double stops into a riff.

note: The guitar-beginner week in the new teaching style: each day is one idea, each why says what the drill trains and why it works, done is a feel, and the week ends with drills the student makes up. Triads and double stops on days 2, 4 and 6 break up the spider and position runs, each one a chord the student already knows, played a new way.

plan.title: Week 1: position 1, clean changes, triads and double stops
plan.summary: A minor pentatonic position 1, G-C-D and power chord changes, and the same chords as triads and double stops, one idea a day. Each drill says what it trains and why, and by day 7 you make up drills of your own.

exercises.title: The spider where position 1 lives
exercises.focus: Frets 5 to 8, one finger per fret, every string, 60 bpm
exercises.why: Position 1 sits at frets 5 to 8, one finger per fret, so warming up right there trains the exact stretch the scale needs.

sections.text: Put finger 1 on the 5th fret of the low E string and the other fingers on the next frets, so finger 4 sits on the 8th. Press Play below to start the metronome, then play the four notes, one note per beat. Do the same on each string up to the high e, then come back down: the tab below shows every note, with the finger under it. Keep going until your hand stays still and only the fingers move.

exercises.title: G, C and D in time
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G changes · down strums at 60 bpm
exercises.why: G, C and D are the 1, 4 and 5 of G major, the three chords most songs lean on, so a clean change between them opens up more music than any new chord.

sections.text: The shapes
Tap a chord box to hear the chord, then fret it as shown. Change between two shapes slowly with your eyes closed, then open them to check every string rings.
In time

Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum down on every beat, one bar per chord, and use beat 4 to move. It's working when the new chord lands on beat 1 without a gap.

exercises.title: Position 1, then your own phrases
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · 60 bpm, the roots, phrases over a band
exercises.why: Every phrase in position 1 sounds finished when it lands on A, so knowing where the three A's are lets you make music from day one.

sections.text: Up and down at 60
Press Play below to start the metronome. Play the position from the low {{1}} up to the high E string and back, one note per beat.
Only the roots
Now only the three {{1}} notes are in play. Hop between them in any order until you can find each one without looking.
Your own phrases
Press Play below to start the band. Make up short phrases from the whole position, with a gap after each, and end every one on a {{1}}. Try ending on another note once, and listen to how it hangs.

days.theme: Root and 5th: power chords and double stops

exercises.title: Spider, new order
exercises.focus: Fingers 1324 at frets 5 to 8, 60 bpm
exercises.why: Changing the finger order makes each finger move on its own, which is what phrases need once they stop going straight up and down.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Play frets 5 to 8 in the order 1, 3, 2, 4 on every string, up and back. Keep it slow enough that every note rings, until the order stops needing thought.

exercises.title: A5, D5, E5
exercises.focus: Power chords A5-D5-E5 · the shape, then split into notes at 70 bpm
exercises.why: A power chord is a root and its 5th, so once your hand knows the one shape, every chord is just a new place for it.

sections.text: One shape, three places
Tap a chord box to hear it. All three are the same shape, moved to a new string or fret. Let only the two fretted strings ring, and mute the rest with the side of your hand.
Split it

Press Play below to start the play-along. Strike the root and 5th together, pick the octave above and the 5th on their own, then strike both again. The tab shows every note. Keep going until the move to the next chord lands on beat 1.

exercises.title: Double stops in position 1
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · two notes at once on the top two strings
exercises.why: Position 1 has two notes at the same fret on the B and high e strings in two places, so the scale you already know holds two double stops, the two-note sound of blues and rock.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the play-along. Play the two notes together, pick two notes on their own, then play the next pair. Follow the tab until the jump between the two pairs feels easy.
Now find both pairs in the position: {{5}} with {{1}}, and {{b7}} with {{b3}}. Play each one, then the single notes around it, and make up a short line that ends on a double stop.

exercises.title: A riff of your own
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · roots and 5ths over drums in A
exercises.why: A riff is a short phrase repeated, so two notes and a rhythm are all you need to make one up.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Make up a short riff from {{1}} and {{5}}, one at a time or both at once as a double stop, and repeat it until it grooves. Then change one thing: the rhythm, the order or the octave.

exercises.title: G to C, smoother each round
exercises.focus: G-C changes · one-minute rounds
exercises.why: The change you repeat is the one your hand learns, so short rounds on one change grow faster than long ones on many.

sections.text: Tap a chord box to hear it. Change between G and C as smoothly as you can for a minute, rest, and go again. Each round, aim to have the next chord ready a little sooner after the strum.

exercises.title: Position 1 at 70, then 80
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · 70 then 80 bpm
exercises.why: Speed comes from playing just a little faster than easy, so step up only once the slower tempo feels relaxed.

sections.text: At 70
Press Play below to start the metronome at 70. Play the position up and down, one note per beat, until it feels relaxed.
At 80
Press Play below to start the metronome at 80. Same position, same {{1}} start. If it feels rushed, go back to 70 for a round.

exercises.title: Call and response
exercises.focus: Position 1 over drums in A · question and answer
exercises.why: A phrase that asks and one that answers is how solos talk, so this turns notes into sentences.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Play a short phrase that ends anywhere (the question), then answer it with one that ends on {{1}}. Keep the answer close to the question, as if replying.

exercises.title: Do Mi Sol tune
exercises.focus: A tune on the notes of the C chord, on the neck
exercises.why: This tune uses only the notes of the C chord, so your fingers learn a chord as a melody.

sections.text: Press Play below to hear the tune and see each note on the neck. Play along until you can hear the next note before you play it.

days.theme: Triads: a chord in three notes

exercises.title: G, C and D as triads
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G triads · strings 3-2-1, then 4-3-2 · 60 bpm
exercises.why: A triad is the three notes that make a chord, so each chord has a small shape on every set of three strings, and moving to a new set is a new drill with the same chords.

sections.text: On the G, B and e strings
Press Play below to start the play-along. Strike the three notes on each beat, one bar per chord, and find each shape on the tab. Play only those three strings, until each new shape lands on beat 1.
On the D, G and B strings
Same chords, one string set lower. The shapes change, the chords don't. Press Play below and play it the same way, then go back to the top strings and hear the difference.

exercises.title: G-Em-C-D strumming
exercises.focus: G-Em-C-D · down strums at 70 bpm
exercises.why: G Em C D is the loop behind countless songs, so a steady strum through it lets you play along with them.

sections.text: The shapes
Tap a chord box to hear it, then fret each one as shown. Change around the loop slowly, until Em to C stops being the slow one.
In time
Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum down on every beat, one bar per chord.

exercises.title: End on a different note
exercises.focus: Position 1 over drums in A · end on A or C
exercises.why: The last note sets the mood of a phrase, so choosing it is the first step to sounding like you mean it.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Play phrases that end on {{1}} (A), then on {{b3}} (C). Listen: A sounds finished, C sounds open and sad. Pick the ending each phrase wants.

exercises.title: Sol La Sol
exercises.focus: A short tune in G, from tab
exercises.why: A tune you can sing in your head is the best check that your hands play what you hear.

sections.text: Press Play below to hear the tune, then play along from the tab. Once it's in your hands, hum it first and then play it without Play.

exercises.title: Spider from the 1st fret
exercises.focus: Fingers 1324 at frets 1 to 4, 70 bpm
exercises.why: Low on the neck the frets are widest, so the same pattern there builds the stretch for open chords.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Play frets 1 to 4 in the order 1, 3, 2, 4 on every string, up and back, until the stretch feels as easy as it did at the 5th fret.

exercises.title: E5, G5, A5 riff
exercises.focus: E5-G5-A5 · down strums at 80 bpm
exercises.why: The power chord shape works on any root, so a riff in E is the same hand you used in A.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum each power chord down on every beat, one bar each, until the slide between them is smooth.

exercises.title: E minor pentatonic, two places
exercises.focus: E minor pentatonic · open and at the 12th fret
exercises.why: A position's shape doesn't change with the key, it just moves, so every shape you know works in all twelve keys.

sections.text: Open position
Press Play below to start the metronome. Play E minor pentatonic in the open position, up and down, starting and ending on {{1}}.
At the 12th fret
The same notes an octave up, in the same shape as position 1 in A. Play it up and down, then hop to the open position and back on the low {{1}}.

exercises.title: Your A phrases in E
exercises.focus: Improvise in E over drums
exercises.why: A phrase is a shape on the neck, so a phrase you made in A plays in E just by moving it.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Take a phrase you made up in A this week and play it here, then make up new ones ending on {{1}}.

days.theme: A riff from triads, notes and double stops

exercises.title: The spider at 80
exercises.focus: Fingers 1234 at frets 3 to 6, 80 bpm
exercises.why: Holding the pattern at a faster tempo shows you how far your hands have come since day 1.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome at 80. Play frets 3 to 6 with fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4 on every string, up and back. Notice what feels easier than on day 1.

exercises.title: G, C and D without looking
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G changes · down strums at 70 bpm
exercises.why: Looking at your hand is a habit, and a change you can make without looking is one you really own.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum along, but look at the chord boxes instead of your hand. When a change goes wrong, slow down in your head, not on the strings.

exercises.title: A riff: triad, two notes, double stop
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G · triads on the top strings, two notes, a double stop · 60 then 70 bpm
exercises.why: A triad and two of its notes are one hand shape, so a riff that mixes them sounds full and never makes your hand jump.

sections.text: G and C at 60
Press Play below to start the play-along. Each bar is the chord's triad, two of its notes picked on their own, and the triad again. Follow the tab until your hand stays in one place.
G, C, D, G at 70
Now D joins, and the last two bars end on a double stop instead of the triad. Once it flows, make it yours: pick two other notes of the chord in the middle of each bar.

exercises.title: A longer tune
exercises.focus: A tune in G · tab at 65, then the neck at 75
exercises.why: Reading it once from tab and once from the neck links the numbers to the places your fingers go.

sections.text: From tab at 65
Press Play below to hear the tune and play along from the tab.
On the neck at 75
Press Play below: now the tune is on the neck, a little faster. Play along until you can play it with your eyes closed.

exercises.title: G-Em-C-D, full pattern
exercises.focus: G-Em-C-D · D . D U . U D U at 80 bpm
exercises.why: This pattern keeps the hand moving down and up on every half beat, so the strings it skips make the groove.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum the pattern on each chord, keeping your hand moving even when it misses the strings, until it swings on its own.

tool.pattern: D . D U . U D U

exercises.title: A position drill of your own
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 in A and E · your own drill
exercises.why: Every drill this week changed one thing (the key, the tempo, the notes in play), so you can make your own by changing one thing yourself.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Make up a drill from position 1: pick one thing to change (the key, which notes are in play, the direction or the rhythm) and play it until it feels easy. Then change another, or add the double stops from day 2.

exercises.title: Jam over Am and G
exercises.focus: Position 1 over Am-G · land on A
exercises.why: Landing on the chord's root as it changes is the simplest way to make a solo follow the chords.

sections.text: Land on A
Press Play below to start the backing. Improvise from position 1 and land on {{1}} when Am comes round.
Your own ending
Keep the backing going and pick your own landing note for each phrase. Listen for the one you like best over G.

exercises.title: Your tune, for the record
exercises.focus: The day 6 tune in G at 75
exercises.why: Playing the week's tune once more shows you what has changed in your hands.

sections.text: Press Play below and play the tune from day 6 along with it. Then play it on your own and change one thing about it: the speed, an octave, or an ending.
